newsitem.title: UK: Israeli embassy bombed to derail peace, court told.
newsitem.headline: Israeli embassy bombed to derail peace, court told.

text.p: A Palestinian housewife drove a car carrying a bomb that badly damaged the Israeli embassy in London in 1994 in a bid to de-rail the Arab-Israeli peace process, prosecution lawyers told a court here on Monday.

David Calvert-Smith alleged Nadia Zekra was a member of a group of middle-class London-based Palestinians who believed that Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat was "misguided in his attempts to come to any accommodation with Israel".
The bomb, which exploded in July 1994, badly damaged the embassy and shattered the windows of nearby houses. No one was injured.

Calvert-Smith told the court Zekra left the bomb in the back or boot of a car which had been parked as close to the Israeli embassy as possible. Zekra, 49, has denied a charge of causing an explosion.

Another woman and two men on trial with Zekra deny charges of conspiracy. They are accused of taking part in the planning and manufacture of the bomb and also of a second bomb which exploded outside a Jewish charitable organisation in London.
The embassy bomb was set off after then Israeli premier Yitzhak Rabin and King Hussein of Jordan signed the Washington Declaration paving the way for peace between their countries.

The same day letters claiming responsibility for the attack were posted to two Arabic newspapers and the Palestine Liberation Organisation's offices in London from a group calling themselves the "Palestine Resistance Jaffa Group in Palestine", Calvert-Smith said.
He said all four defendants "are of Palestinian origin and are well integrated into English society and the middle and upper middle classes".
All apart from Zekra had been to British universities and their knowledge helped in the creation of the bombs, he added.
Jurors were warned by the judge before the start of the trial to put the Middle East conflict out of their minds and try the case purely on the evidence in court.
